zone: Upper Sauk River road — Mount Pugh, Bedal Creek and the Sloan Creek side
_areas_note: THREE trailheads, all hanging off the stretch of the Mountain Loop that runs south from Darrington rather than off the paved western half. (1) The MOUNT PUGH trailhead at the end of Forest Road 2095, about twelve and a half miles south of Darrington and then a mile and a half up the spur. (2) The BEDAL CREEK road, Forest Road 4096, which climbs steeply for two rough miles from a junction roughly a mile south of Bedal Campground, seven miles north of Barlow Pass. (3) The SLOAN CREEK and NORTH FORK SAUK side, reached by turning east on Forest Road 49 about sixteen miles south of Darrington and following it six and a half miles to Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk trailhead. TWO PEAKS REMOVED, both because they are not served by any of those three roads. SITKUM SPIRE is not a peak at all in the sense this grouping assumes — its coordinate falls on Glacier Peak's own west summit ridge, a rock finger beside the saddle at around 9,500 ft on the Sitkum Glacier route, so it is a feature of Glacier Peak reached from the White Chuck side or from high on the mountain, and the Glacier Peak file already carries its camp. MOUNT SAUL is in Chelan County on Wenatchee Ridge, south of the White River and north of Indian Creek; its standard route starts in the White River valley off the Lake Wenatchee side and uses the Indian Creek and Airplane Lake trails, which is a different national forest, a different drive, and about as far from the Sauk road as a Glacier Peak Wilderness peak can be. KOLOLO PEAKS WAS CHECKED AND KEPT, but only just, and for a specific reason: it really is approached from the North Fork Sauk trailhead at the end of Forest Road 49, which is one of this file's declared trailheads. It is a twelve to thirteen mile walk from that road end over White Pass and Foam Pass to the White Chuck Glacier, so most of its approach camps belong to the Glacier Peak file and are not repeated here. BEDAL PEAK WAS ALSO CONFIRMED. Its removal from a Stillaguamish grouping in an earlier pass was correct — the Bedal Creek road leaves the loop on the Sauk side well beyond Barlow Pass, and the peak shares its road with Sloan rather than with anything on the north side. PAINTED MOUNTAIN, also mapped as Red Mountain, is correctly here: its trail leaves from the Sloan Creek Campground area and it is a day objective with no camp of its own, which is stated below rather than papered over. NOT DUPLICATED from the earlier files: Bedal Campground, the Sloan Peak high camp, Mackinaw Shelter, the White Pass and Foam Creek benches, Glacier Gap, and Boulder Basin above Sitkum Creek.

sites.name: Mount Pugh road end, Forest Road 2095
sites.capacity: Car bivy only, and a thin one. Parking is a few turnouts along the last of the spur rather than a car park, with no sites, no tables and no toilet. Half a dozen vehicles fills it and there is nowhere to overflow to without blocking the road.
sites.water: None at the road end and none for the first mile and a half of trail. Everything gets carried up from the valley or drawn at the lake above.
sites.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, and the trailhead itself sits OUTSIDE designated wilderness — Glacier Peak Wilderness begins high on the mountain above Stujack Pass, not at the road. Reports differ on whether a fee pass is enforced at this particular trailhead; a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass costs nothing extra to carry and settles the question. No self-issue permit at the road. Seasonal forest-wide fire restrictions apply and from midsummer normally mean no open flame.
sites.notes: The staging point for MOUNT PUGH, which most parties climb in a single long day from here — around five and a half miles and well over five thousand feet to the summit, with the character changing three times on the way. Forest and stream crossings to the lake at a mile and a half, then a steady climb to the pass, then a rough exposed ridge with a genuine scrambling section around the head of a small remnant glacier before it eases to the top. Sleeping at the car is the honest plan for that day: the spur is short enough that a party staying at any of the valley campgrounds can drive up in the dark, and the trail's first miles are straightforward walking that goes quickly by headtorch. The spur climbs steeply and is rough in places but is normally passable to an ordinary car driven with care. The road in from Darrington is the county-maintained section of the loop and stays open through the year to the seasonal gate further south, which puts this trailhead on the right side of the winter closure — but it is landslide ground and has been blocked outright by a slide within recent memory, so confirm before driving from any distance rather than assuming. Season for the peak is roughly July into October; the ridge above the pass with snow on it is a mountaineering proposition rather than a scramble.

sites.name: Lake Metan, Mount Pugh trail
sites.capacity: A few primitive spots in the trees on the short spur down to the lake — two or three tents on flat, well-used forest ground, with no built structures of any kind.
sites.water: The lake, and this is the LAST WATER on the entire route. Nothing above it is dependable, and above the pass there is nothing at all except late-lying snow. Fill everything here going up and note it for the descent.
sites.permit: National forest outside designated wilderness at this elevation, so no wilderness permit, no quota and no party-size limit for camping here. A Northwest Forest Pass covers the vehicle. Fires are subject to whatever seasonal restrictions are in force and are usually prohibited from midsummer; carry a stove regardless, because this is a small lake basin that takes heavy day-hiker traffic and does not need fire rings.
sites.notes: A mile and a half and about thirteen hundred feet up from the road end, on a short signed spur off the main trail, this is the only established camping on the Pugh approach and it turns a punishing day into a manageable one. Its real value is for a party that wants the ridge above Stujack Pass in the cool of the morning without a two-hour drive and a headtorch start, or for one that arrives too late in the day to sensibly begin. It buys about a third of the climbing but leaves the hardest two thirds — a further two and a half miles to the pass and then the ridge — for the summit day, so treat it as a soft first night rather than a high camp. The setting is wooded and enclosed, mosquito-heavy in early summer and cold in the shade well into the morning. Snow lingers around the lake into June in an ordinary year. Because it is the last water, an efficient party often does not sleep here at all but stops for twenty minutes to load up, and that is a perfectly good use of the place.

sites.name: Stujack Pass and the benches just below it
sites.capacity: Small and rough — a couple of tents at most on gravel and heather pockets in the saddle and on the shelves a little below it on the approach side. Nothing established, no flat platform, and no shelter of any kind from wind.
sites.water: NONE, and this is the defining constraint. There is no source at or near the pass. Late-lying snow patches on the north side can be melted early in the season and are gone by August, after which every litre comes up from the lake nearly two and a half miles and two and a half thousand feet below.
sites.permit: The pass itself is the boundary — camping in the saddle sits at the very edge of GLACIER PEAK WILDERNESS, and the ridge and summit above are inside it. Where wilderness applies, so does the free self-issue permit from the trailhead box and the twelve-person party limit counting people and stock together. No fires: this is thin subalpine ground with no wood and nothing that recovers from a scar. Northwest Forest Pass at the road.
sites.notes: This is a high bivouac rather than a camp, and it exists for one purpose — putting a party on the exposed upper ridge of MOUNT PUGH at first light rather than in the afternoon, when the scrambling section around the head of the small glacier is more pleasant and the weather is more predictable. From the saddle the remaining mile and a half of ridge is rough, narrow in places and genuinely exposed, and it is much better done rested and early than at the end of a five-thousand-foot day from the car. The trade is severe and should be weighed honestly: you carry all your water up, you camp on ground with nothing to hide behind, and the pass funnels wind hard enough to make a marginal forecast miserable. Anyone who is not committed to the summit is better off at the lake. Snow holds on the north side of the pass and in the gullies below it long after the trail lower down is clear, and an early-season party will be kicking steps to reach it. In a thunderstorm this is the wrong place to be — the ridge above is the highest ground for some way and there is no descent that is quick. Camp on gravel or bare rock, not on the heather, which is thin and slow to come back.

sites.name: Bedal Basin, below the north side of Bedal Peak
sites.capacity: A meadow basin with room for several small parties on durable ground near the boulders, though flat spots are fewer than the open look of the place suggests. It is quiet — this trail sees very little traffic and you can have the basin to yourself on a summer weekend.
sites.water: Bedal Creek and its meltwater feeders run through the basin and are reliable through the climbing season, thinning late in a hot August. The creek is crossed twice on the way up and both crossings are straightforward by midsummer but pushy in snowmelt.
sites.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS, which begins about half a mile up the trail — free self-issue wilderness permit from the box at the road end, no reservation and no quota, and a twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass to leave a vehicle. Fires are legal in principle at this elevation but inappropriate in a small meadow basin with limited dead wood, and summer restrictions usually prohibit them outright; carry a stove.
sites.notes: The high camp for BEDAL PEAK, sitting directly under its steep north side and its cliffs, and the only sensible place to sleep for a party attempting the peak rather than just visiting the basin. Getting here is about two and a half miles from the road end at around 2,800 ft, climbing steadily through old forest and across avalanche tracks, and the trail deteriorates as it goes — it receives very little maintenance, is thickly overgrown in the avalanche chutes by midsummer, and effectively gives out about a mile and a half in, after which the way is up the rocky creek bed and through thin forest into the basin. Expect brush, wet feet and route-finding rather than a walk. The basin holds the remains of a pioneer cabin among the boulders, which makes a useful landmark for orienting the last of the approach. The peak above needs route-finding and, on most lines, real climbing rather than scrambling, so the short approach should not be read as a short day. The spur road itself is the other constraint: two steep, rough miles where high clearance is genuinely wanted rather than merely advised. Bedal Campground sits a mile down the main loop road from the junction and is the drive-in fallback for a party that arrives too late to start up the spur, and it is already recorded in the earlier upper-loop file. Snow lies in the basin into July.

sites.name: Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk road end
sites.capacity: A small primitive campground of a handful of sites in the trees beside the trailhead, with a vault toilet and little else — no hookups, no host, no reservations. Being the road end for several long trips, the parking beside it fills before the sites do.
sites.water: No potable supply. Sloan Creek and the North Fork Sauk both run close by and filter fine; this is clean valley water with none of the old-mine metals problem that spoils the drainages further west.
sites.permit: The campground and the road end sit just outside GLACIER PEAK WILDERNESS, which the trails enter shortly above. Free self-issue wilderness permit from the box at the trailhead for anything going up, twelve-person party limit counting people and stock together. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the vehicle. Fires in the existing rings only, and forest-wide summer restrictions routinely close even those from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
sites.notes: The staging point for the eastern half of this zone and the drive-in night before two very different trips. PAINTED MOUNTAIN, which older maps and signs call Red Mountain, goes from right here as a DAY OBJECTIVE with no established camp anywhere on it: a mile of maintained trail to about 3,100 ft, then a short steep step of dirty ledges that is real scrambling, then a faint intermittent path along the southwest ridge past the site of a long-gone lookout, then scree to a summit just under seven thousand feet — roughly eight miles round trip for nearly five thousand feet of gain, which is a full day from the car and the reason this campground matters. KOLOLO PEAKS is the opposite kind of trip and starts from the same place: twelve to thirteen miles up the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass and beyond, with its camps already recorded in the Glacier Peak file. The access road is the honest caveat here. It is rough, with washout sections around the first and sixth miles where high clearance is strongly wanted, and it has a recent history of closures — a landslide on the main loop road cut off the junction entirely through one winter, and a lightning-caused fire in the drainage closed the road, this campground and both trailheads for two months of one autumn. That fire stayed small and its closure has lapsed, but burnt ground above a trail means deadfall and loose footing for years afterwards. Confirm the road with the district before the drive; this is not a place to discover a gate.

sites.name: White Chuck Glacier basin, under Kololo Peaks
sites.capacity: Open bare-ground bivouac sites scattered through the basin, with room for several parties and no crowding — this is a big, empty place. Rock-walled windbreaks left by previous parties are the nearest thing to a built site.
sites.water: Meltwater streams and ponds through the basin, running all through the climbing season and often silty. Late in a hot summer the flow drops to a trickle off the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time. Everybody camped here drinks it, so site the toilet well away from it.
sites.permit: GLACIER PEAK WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit collected at the North Fork Sauk trailhead box, twelve-person party limit. No fires: this is bare rock, pumice and snow above treeline with nothing to burn and nothing that recovers. Human waste is carried out or buried properly well away from the meltwater. Northwest Forest Pass at the road.
sites.notes: The climbing camp for KOLOLO PEAKS, and the reason Kololo is a three-day trip rather than a weekend scramble. It sits in the stark rock-and-snow basin on the edge of what remains of the White Chuck Glacier, reached from the North Fork Sauk road end by twelve or thirteen miles of walking — the long river approach, then the steep switchbacking climb to White Pass, then east on the crest trail and out along the Foam Basin path toward Foam Pass. Eight hours from the road to camp is a normal rather than a slow time for a party carrying overnight gear. From here the peaks themselves are straightforward, a walk on glacier remnant and snow followed by easy scrambling on rubbly volcanic rock, and moving from one summit to the next is simple. The glacier is the thing to understand: it has retreated further and faster than almost anything in the range and much of what maps show as ice is now bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds, with the surviving ice thin, hard and holed by open crevasses late in the season. That means crampons rather than a snow plod by September, and it means route descriptions written twenty years ago describe a surface that is gone. This is deliberately the only Kololo camp recorded here — the lower camps on the same approach, at the river bench, at White Pass and at the gap above this basin, all belong to the Glacier Peak file and are not repeated. Exposed ground with no shelter, confusing in fog, and a long way from help.
